newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: U.S. pushes for technology deal at WTO meeting.
newsitem.headline: U.S. pushes for technology deal at WTO meeting.

text.p: U.S. officials were pushing on Sunday to seal a global pact to eliminate tariffs on information technology which they hope will be the crowning achievement of the World Trade Organisation's first ministerial meeting.

U.S. and European Union (EU) officials met on the eve of the five-day WTO meeting to try to thrash out differences that remain on the Information Technology Agreement (ITA), which would eliminate tariffs on a wide range of computer and telecommunications technology by 2000.
"We are making some very important progress," Barshefsky told reporters. "The work is going on quite intensively. It will remain intense throughout the week."
But she declined to say whether a final deal is close at hand. U.S. and EU officials said a series of intense bilateral discussions will be held this week in hopes of winning a deal.
Top trade officials from 128 nations are set to meet in Singapore from Monday. The meeting will conclude on Friday.

A Japanese official told reporters that working-level discussions among the four major trade partners -- The United States, Japan, Canada and European Union -- were "in gear". A major consideration, he said, is how many countries can be persuaded to participate.

Barshefsky expressed concern about Europe's commitment to the agreement. She told reporters there were indications that the Europeans felt completion of the ITA hinged upon an acceptable final declaration to be issued by the WTO ministers at the end of this week's meeting. She added that she saw no linkage between the ITA and the WTO declaration.
A European official, however, expressed hope earlier on Sunday that differences between the EU and United States will be resolved by the end of the week.
"I would hope you will find a coming together of the European and United States fairly soon so we can push the others," said the European source, who declined to be named.
U.S. negotiators say they want a "broad" agreement covering a wide range of products, estimated to be worth up to $1 trillion a year in world trade.

But they want to exclude fibre optics, graphic display tubes, photocopiers and capacitors -- circuits used in electronic goods. The Europeans have balked at those exclusions, but feel a deal can be done.

"We both hope this is going to be a really concrete thing, a nugget...if not finally agreed, then laid out to be agreed later," the European source told Reuters. "A deal is within reach. We have to push very, very hard."
The source said both sets of negotiators realised the importance of coming to an acceptable agreement this week, even if the final signing was delayed until later.
"Whatever deal is done -- a deal now or a bankable deal for later -- the work will have to be done now at the WTO," he said.
Both the United States and European Union have said they need a "critical mass" of information technology producing and consuming countries to sign on to the accord, before it can be agreed.
The EU has said it has a "priority list" of 16 core non-European states it wants to join the deal but stresses the list may be expanded to other states.
The current list covers Australia, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, Korea, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, the Philippines, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand and the United States.
